div.p: In the article an approach to modeling and verification of real-time systems is presented. Specfication PEARL description language in used for HW / SW modeling. It has its origins in the standard Multiprocessor PEARL language. Its usefulness has been enhanced for asymmetrical multiprocessor system modeling and parameters for schedulability analysis have been added. It is meant to be an over-layer for PEARL programs and supports the corresponding program model. The detailed program models are represented internally by Timed State Transition Automata. The model of the co-designed system is verified for feasibility with co-simulation. The resulting information may be used for changes in the current design to gain a feasible model of the system. Afrer that the program models may be enhanced to their full functionality. Schedulability analysis, which should provide the designer with more precise timing information, shall then be done. The new timing information can be reused on the system model in order to discover bottlenecks or possible discrepancies with the estimated times. By utilising this methodology the possibility of implementing an infeasible system should be minimised.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time systems are expected to conform to additional safety restrictions beside the real-time imposed limitations. Therefore it is necessary to design them in a way, which will enable effective verification of their correctness.

To enable verification, often formal languages and/or mathematical notations are used, for which subsequently a proof can be worked out (e.g.: differential equations' supported formalisms, which describe the system's operation in time and space [6], formal languages and timed automata 11, 31, combinations of conventional CASE methods and state cham [20], graphical techniques with the same expressing power as their formal language counterparts [5]). While enabling formal verification most of these methods lack the versatility of basic constructs and user friendliness. Therefore graphical formalisms with a greater set of baqic constructs have been defined (e.g.: CSWCCSR [ll], TTM/RTTL [14], LACATRE [ 19]>, while keeping enough "strictness" to enable verification. Dedicated state transition automata like CRSM [18] are often used as the basic internal computation model (e.g.: LACATRE, POLIS [2]).

For pragmatical reasons simulation is often used to check the correctness of the designed system or parts thereof. CO-designing systems with time limitations led to the introduction of real-time scheduling algorithms into their co-design and implementation (e.g. [ 121).

A good example for the wide variety of verification methods, which can be used for embedded real-time systems, is the VHDL language, for which verification methods have been devised, ranging from formal methods to co-simulation and combinations thereof (e.g.: [ 10,201).

div.head: Specification PEARL methodology
div.p: Our co-design method originates from the standard Multiprocessor PEARL [ 171 specification language, which was developed to support the specification and programming of distributed multiprocessor systems using the PEARL language [15, 161. Specification PEARL extends the Multiprocessor PEARL specification language, in a manner foreseen by the standard, with additional properties to enable the construction of asymmetrical architectures and later schedulability analysis. It enables the construction of a conceptual system model, whereby its hardware and software architectures may be designed in parallel.

div.head: Our related work encompasses schedulability analysis
div.p: of PEARL programs with a constrained subset of PEARL constructs to enable execution time analysis. A corresponding RTOS (Real-Time Operating System) kemel was built to support the program model and system calls of PEARL [4].

The Specification PEARL methodology enables the construction of a system model, which is then combined with the RTOS and verified for its feasibility by cosimulation. Based on the results of the simulation the system model may be adjusted accordingly. A feasible system model may then be enhanced to its full functionality and checked with schedulability analysis to obtain the most accurate timing information. The results of the CO-simulation retain their value, if the -timing parameters remain unchanged during the enhancement to the systems' full functionality.

div.head: Specification PEARL language properties
div.p: The proposed Specification PEARL methodology has the following characteristics, usually required for codesign methods and specification languages: abstraction; i.e., insignificant details are suppressed, the conceptual world of. the application domain is supported, and no implementation is referred to; application concepts and structures, relations and sequences are easily recognisable, easy readability, but nevertheless precise notation, provision for unambiguous and complete descriptions of requirements and design, support for effective communication between clients, designers and users about the system to be developed, the possibility of extending specifications into executable prototypes, systematic integration of the specification method into the whole development process, and U intermediate design checking as well as system
In addition Specification PEARL has inherited the 0 constructs for the description of hardware configurations, 0 constructs for the description of software configurations,

U constructs for the specification of communication and its characteristics (peripheral and process connections, physical and logical connections, transmission protocols), as well as Cl constructs for specifying both conditions and the method of carrying out dynamic reconfigurations in cases of failure.

The leading motives for using the Specification PEARL methodology are: model verification before implementation. following properties from Multiprocessor PEARL: 0 the modelling (specification) language and the PEARL language programming language are syntactically and conceptually closely related, 0 the ability to use the SW specifications as program prototypes as well as extend them to fully functional programs easily, 0 early reasoning on system integration, 0 the ability to apply timing parameters to hardware 0 the ability to simulate the modelled solution and and software constructs, and check its feasibility before implementation.

div.head: Specification PEARL language concepts
div.p: The notation of the specification language consists of textual and graphical constructs, which may be used interchangeably [7,91. The cornerstones of the hardware model are STATIONS, being the processing nodes of a di:itributd or a multiprocessor system. Their components may be chosen from a list of general hardware components like processors (PROCTYPES), memories (WORKSTORES) or DEVICES (INTERFACES, TIMERS, PORTS, etc.). These components determine the structure of STATIONS and their interconnections. On the other hand, their properties also represent the necessary timing information for later verification and schedulability analysis.

The main building blocks of the software model are COLLECTIONS of TASKS, which are mapped to the STATIONS of the hardware model, depending on their state information. In general multiple COLLECTIONS of TASKS may exist for each of the STATIONS' states, to which they are mapped. The TASKS are represented by Timed State Transition Diagrams (TSTD), which represent their dynamical behaviour. They are also assigned properties (e.g.: trigger conditions, response times or priorities for their scheduling, PORT ulappingii for interta5k communication, etc.).
The two models are glued together by the RTOS, supporting the tasking model of the PEARL lalnguage, being the chosen programming language for our TASKS.

div.head: Verification method
div.p: Our verification method is based on co-simulation with EDF scheduling and time boundaries [7, 81. It is primarily meant for checking the timing properties of the niodelletl system in order to determine its feasibility. The designed system model is transformed into an internal representation for simulation, whose primary result is a successful execution or failure, whereas the secondary result is its execution trace, from which adlditional information can be extracted. This information is then used for discovering bottlenecks and unreachable state!; and resources in the designed prototypes.
For a successful verification, it is assumed that the system model is complete and consistent. Intermediate checks must be done during the design of the system architecture to ensure this:

Completeness check (all components, which are referred to, are present and fully described); Range and compatibility check (some parameters of components may be range checked to discover obvious mistakes and to discover possible incompatibilities in the parameters of the interconnected componenb); Software to hardware mapping check (every COLLECTION must be mapped onto a STATIONS' state considering its and / or its supervisors' resources'; e.g.: the number of tasks, which may be handled by a single RTOS processing node is limited). These checks are the preparation for the integration verification, which is described in the forthcoming sections.

div.head: System model
div.p: Our system model is an internal representation of the system, which is joined with the simulators structures for verification. The internal hardware model consists of processing nodes representing STATIONS, having the specified properties. The components of STATIONS are not modelled separately, instead they are represented by the properties of the processing nodes. The internal software model COLLECTIONS are mapped to the STATION'S nodes of the hardware model based on their (initial) state. The COLLECTION nodes are linked lists of TASK representing nodes with references to their intemal TSTD representation.
Verification is done based on the following presumptions:
0 There is only one global simulation clock in the system and all Real-Time Clocks (RTCs) are synchronised with it;

U The time events relate to the corresponding STATIONS' RTC; 0 Tasks are assigned deadlines for their execution (the only exception are short initialisation tasks); 0 Task states (TSTD elements) have the following timing properties: 0 Time frame for the activity being performed within the state (in RTC time units), 0 The time units necessary to perform the activity (in RTC units); it is set by the designer I programmer based on his I her experience or by employing an execution time analyser for the specified STATION, in which case a much more precise estimate is gained.

The RTOS has an important role in the co-simulation, even though the emphasis is not on it. Our RTOS supports the tasking model and system calls of the PEARL programming language. It supports the deadline (Earliest Deadline First) and priority driven scheduling strategies. Its resources are parameterised (e.g.: number of tasks, synchronisers, signals, events, queued events, etc.). The parameterisation of the RTOS is done by setting the properties of the KERNEL STATION.

div.head: An illustrative example
div.p: Let's consider a typical automation examplethe railroad crossing problem. Lets say, we have a railroad crossing with two tracks and we want to automate the barriers so they are closed, when the train comes in The barriers are synchronised through a common controlling device, while receiving the signals from sensors on each side of the railroad crossing. In the following sections this example will be modelled from different points of view and referred to as the Example.

div.head: HW model
div.p: There are three possible different kinds of processing nodes in the system architecture: BASIC (general purpose affecting the duration of TSTD states, but also used in the schedulability analysis, memory size, access type and time, are all used in the detailed execution time analysis, transmission rates of interfaces are used to calculate the duration of TRANSMIT and RECEIVE operations between STATIONS during state duration estimation and execution time analysis.

Fig. 3 shows an example HW architecture description for the mentioned Example with its corresponding translation into the intemal representation. The sensors are modelled by the peripheral STATIONS S1 and S2, which are hooked to the KP KERNEL STATION, supervising the barrier controlling TASK STATIONS TP1 andTP2.

div.head: SW model
div.p: As shown in Fig. 4, the COLLECTIONS are represented internally by linked lists of TASK nodes. Initialisation TASK nodes reside at the beginning of this list, which is not ordered in any other way. COLLECTION nodes are associated with specific STATIONS and their states by bi-directional links. Each TASK node has a bi-directional reference to the start of the TSTD node, representing the body of the task.
At the same time for inter-TASK (COLLECTION) communication between different STATIONS their PORTS are used, hence referencing the HW model.

Considering the Example to which also Fig. 4 relates, there are three collections, each associated with its STATION node. KP-WS represents the RTOS, executed by the KERNEL STATION, whereas TPLWS and TP2-WS represent the program part of both TASK STATIONS, controlling the barriers. They are synchronised through common structures and signals of the KP-WS. They share the status variable, which tells, whether the barrier is open or closed and send / receive each others signals, when they are notified that the train has reached the sensor, announcing its arrival / departure. The signals must come in the consecutive order, because otherwise the first precondition of the Example would be violated.
The TASK T1 (TSTD) model for barrier control is shown in Fig. 5. The same TSTD model pertains to both barriers (their TASKS / COLLECTIONS).

div.head: Task (TSTD) model
div.p: TASKs are represented by Timed State Transition Diagrams [7, 81 (Fig. 5). Timed STDs behave like Timed Finite State Automata and consist of: 0 start states (representing task trigger conditions; separate states for each different trigger condition), 0 transient states (having continuation preconditions, timeout condition, on-timeout action, actions to be performed within the current state) and 0 final states (representing finalisation actions, and an optional return to start state action).

The structure of a TASK is represented by the entry / exit points / states and action states of a TSTD. Since the state transition conditions relate to the system / OS internal states they are formed around system calls, changing these states. Of course they have to outline the TASKs structure together with its control structixes and conditions, which may also represent the stater;' continuation conditions.
For the co-simulation the execution times of individual states need to be estimated. The TASK execution time is calculated based on the longest path in the corresponding TSTD.
Fig. 5 represents the TSTD form of the tasks TI L and T2 in our Example. It is triggered by the signal from one of the peripheral devices, announcing the arrival of the train.

After it has started, the first working state "Close:" ha5 to make sure, that the barrier is closed before the train arrives. The time limit for its execution is d-min, and its expected execution time is d-close. The precondition to the next working state "Train" is the fact, whether the barrier is closed. This state has no explicit deadline although its expected execution time is 2*d_niin. We might say that unless the train stops in the crossing, setting its deadline to 3*d-min, would be a safe assumption. The third working state "Open" has the signal from the opposite side of the barrier as the precondition, meaning that the train has left, and that the barrier must be opened. Its expected execution time i:j d-open and its deadline 2*d_open. If all went well, the final state, having the status that the barrier is open as it!; precondition, ends the task. Otherwise the execution ends in one of the other final states, representing eicecution timeouts, triggering alarms.

div.head: RTOS model
div.p: A small RTOS kernel was developed in the framework of the virtual machine executing the system calls of the program tasks, being analysed on the given architecture.
The executive role of the operating system in the: system model has been retained.
RTOS is assumed to operate within the KERNEL STATION nodes. If such a station does not exist in the system it is executed by the station, executing the application program model (BASIC).

Each RTOS processing node maintains a Real-Time Clock (RTC) for its client nodes. All of these clocks need to be synchronised with the global simulation clock during verification. It services the system calls, whereas the time needed to do this is considered as being included in the time frame of the calling TASKS state. Its sole function is to change the system state and trigger task states, whose trigger conditions relate to the internal data structures of the (operating) system.

The time, which is required to execute the operating system itself (schedule and dispatch cycle) is assumed to be constant and is not considered separately. It is assumed not to affect the speed or rate of application program processing. This assumption is not too hard because we may have a separate OS processing node for each application program node and this time may be considered as being part of the system call service time, since every system call generally requires both mentioned operations.

div.head: Criteria function
div.p: Every verification or validation method requires the definition of a criteria function, which tells, when a system fails, i.e. what the limits of the "normal" execution of the system, being checked, are.
The concept of correctness for the described method of verification has been defined as follows:
"The system fails in the case when during cosimulation:

0 the system reaches an undefined state or 0 its predefined time frame is violated and no timeout-By taking the shortest and longest transition times through the TASK states (TSTD) of the system, it is assumed that enough time domain can be covered to be able to generalise the results to an arbitrary transition time of every state and herewith also the system as a whole. action is defined."

div.head: Integration of simulation with EDF scheduling for verification
div.p: For the verification simulation with next critical event technique and EDF scheduling is used.

The station clock rate is translated into the step size (in RTC units) of the station in the simulation and is used when the next event time is being calculated. As already mentioned, the existing internal devices of STATIONS are not relevant for the co-simulation. They may be subject to compatibility checks and their time parameters may be used later on in the timing and schedulability analysis.

The top level simulation units are STATION nodes. They are COLLECTION nodes' parent nodes. All COLLECTIONS nodes, attached to the same STATION node, form a linked list with references to COLLECTIONS' TASK nodes also forming a linked list.
The basic simulation units are TASK states, representing the atomic operations in the system. They are forming the TSTD internal representation, whose parent node is the TASK node.

The time instant of the next critical moment is always determined by the simulation unit whose critical time is the closest. This time is forwarded to its parent units and finally it becomes the next global critical moment. Simulation is done on the next critical moment basis.

Typically, on each step the tasks are rescheduled by the EDF scheduler. It is checked, whether timing or synchronisation errors have occurred. A transition into a "timeout state" (taken upon violation of the states' timeout condition) represents a controlled program fault. Herewith a transition is done into a final state, from which there is no further transition. If upon the same error this transition is not defined for the current state, the system fails and the error is reported. Otherwise the transition into the next state is always done in two variants (minimum and maximum time), if the preconditions for the transition are fulfilled. The execution protocol is logged instantly.

div.head: EDF next event scheduling
div.p: on the following timing information (see Fig. 2):

Earliest Deadline First next event scheduling is based A : task activation time, R : accumulated task run time (updated with the next critical event), E : task end time (the time when the normal task end is expected based on its maximum run time; upon a context switch the current time t l needs to be remembered, because when the task is re-run this parameter needs to be reset based on the current time t2 and the following formula: Et=E+(t2-tl)), D: task deadline (set, when A is known).

Rescheduling is done when a task is activated due to a scheduled event or on request. The task with the earliest deadline is chosen for the execution and its current state is assigned the current time t as its next critical moment (NOW). Tasks are scheduled to be executed on events, which represent internal states of the system or its operating system. These represent the tasks trigger conditions.

While rescheduling the following criteria (failure conditions) need to be checked for all tasks: t < Z=D-(E-(A+R)), where Z represents the last time when the task needs to start/continue in order to meet its deadline; E < D must be true for all active tasks, since otherwise they have missed their deadlines.

div.head: Co-simulation and EDF next event scheduling
div.p: When initialised all non-scheduled tasks are set the. Z parameter as their next critical moment. The initialisation tasks are run and E and D parameters are set for each active task. They are checked at each critical moment.

The concepts of Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling are integrated into the next event cosimulation by setting the next critical moment for the tasks to the following times: TO : t + minT. T1: t + maxT, where t is the current value of the Real-Time Clock (RTC) and minT and maxT represent minimum and maximum TASK state execution times respectively.

TO and T1 also represent rescheduling points. After the corresponding critical moment (TO or T1) is reached, the next state's pre-condition and the time frame of the state's activities are checked. Additionally the E and Z parameters are checked: E : if the task is active (needs to be updated with each context switchrepresents normal task endif in another state an error has occurred in the simulation), Z : if the task is inactive (represents a missed deadline).

If the result is correct in both cases, the simulation may continue in the following state. Otherwise, or if 2 or E have been reached in a non-final state, the corresponding "timeout" I "deadline miss" action needs to be taken.

div.head: The course of simulation
div.p: Simulation is initialised by resetting the parameters of the processing nodes, initialising the TASK parameters for the scheduler and setting the simulation clock and RTCs to their initial value. The simulation trace channels are reset. The initialisation TASKS may now be run, and to achieve this their next critical moment is set to the current time t (NOW).

During the co-simulation for each state the time of progression to the next state is calculated considering the speed of the STATION'S processing unit (i.e.: its basic cycle length). When the corresponding critical moment is reached, it is checked if herewith the given time frame for the current state has been violated, which results in the following consequences: (1) subtraction of the overhead from the TASK'S slack time, (2) possible progress into a special exception state or (3) task deadline is missed and the system fails.

The results of the simulation are logged dming the execution of every simulation unit and each step is accounted for also within all parent simulation units. This means that every TASK state logs its action into the TASK log, whereas the TASK logs its beginning and end into the COLLECTION log. The COLLECTION logs the time when it was first allocated at the STATION and possible subsequent reloads and the changes of states., which triggered them, into the STATION log. The STATIONS also log the times when they were: communicating among each other (their resources have: been requested) and the times when they were active .. executing tasks.

div.head: The interpretation of results
div.p: If the simulation run resulted in a failure, the: simulation trace is checked and the corresponding adjustments are made to the system model while the: problems persist. It must also be checked to discover bottlenecks and not-visited states.
The simulation trace analysis must be done m,anually. since, except for the failures, other weaknesses of the design like bottlenecks can not be discovered automatically.

The feasibility estimate, which is produced by cosimulation, retains its value, if the foreseen execution times have been chosen correctly (Le.: the circumstances on the time scale do not change when the program part is extended to the fully functional program prototype). Detailed schedulability analysis is not included in the presented verification method. It is foreseen that the schedulability analysis is done subsequentlyafter the mentioned extension of the program part by the programmer.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In the article some (CO-) design methodologies and formalisms used for real-time systems design and verification are compared. The Specification PEARL real-time system hardware / software co-design and verification methodology is presented.

The structure of the models of the hardware and software portions of a system, used during the veri.hcation process, is given. The concepts and mechanisms of our verification method are explained. CO-simulation with EDF next event scheduling is introduced in the verification part of the methodology.
Since simulation is used, the results and their usefulness for the construction of the system model and later schedulability analysis are explained.
The goal of the methodology is to be able to determine the a priori fea5ibility of a program prototype on the given hardware architecture without the need to implement them first.
